h1: Importing wine into India: how the process works
title: Importing Wine into India: The Process | Craft Beer School
desc: How importing wine into India works at process level: customs, import registration, state licences, labels, storage and distribution plus who to work with.
teaser: Wine crosses a central border and then a state one. Both have their own paperwork.
standfirst: Importing wine into India involves central rules at the port and state rules inland. This guide explains the sequence at process level and the advisers you will need.
sections:
The central government handles the border. It sets customs duty on imported goods and requires the importer to be registered for import. Food safety rules apply to imported wine as to other food products.

The state handles everything after that. Alcohol is a state subject, so licences to hold, move and sell wine, excise duty and pricing rules differ from state to state and change. Some states, including Bihar and Gujarat, ban alcohol altogether.

A shipment can clear customs and still sit in a bonded warehouse because the state side is not ready. Sort both layers before you ship.

The importer is the Indian company that brings in the wine. It holds the registrations and licences and bears the legal responsibility. A foreign producer rarely imports directly. Most work with an Indian importer or set up a local company with the right licences.

Customs brokers handle port clearance. Licensing advisers and lawyers deal with the state. A logistics partner moves wine in temperature-controlled transport where possible. Heat damages wine fast. An Indian summer in an unventilated container can ruin a shipment.

• Choose the importer and confirm its licences and registrations
  • Choose the state or states where the wine will be sold
  • Check label requirements, including languages, statements and any state approval
  • Register the brand with the state authority where the state requires it
  • Arrange shipping and insurance with temperature control in mind
  • Clear customs through a broker, paying duty as set at the time
  • Move wine into licensed storage and then to licensed sellers
  • Keep records of each movement for the excise authority

Each step has its own forms and timing. Do not treat the list as a checklist for compliance. It is a map of the places where you need an adviser.

Labels should carry the information central and state rules require. Some states approve labels before sale. Requirements change, so check the current notification for each state. A label printed abroad may need a local sticker for the Indian importer details.

Register your trademark in India. Names are often taken in one category or another. An expensive shipment under a name you cannot protect is a bad start.

Duties and state margins raise the price at the shelf. The gap between producer price and shelf price can be large. Work from your adviser's current figures state by state and test whether customers will pay.

Distribution depends on state rules. Some states route sales through state-run outlets, others through private shops, bars and hotels. Our guide on market research for a new wine brand shows how to test demand before you ship. Our note on winery licensing steps gives the licensing logic for producers inside India.

We help wine producers and importers plan an entry: comparing states, mapping the licensing and import steps to take to your advisers, assessing storage and cold chain and testing the market. Remote work by video call and shared data, with site visits by arrangement.

We are not customs brokers, lawyers or licensing agents. We work alongside them. We do not quote duties, promise a licence or name clients.

Wine is more forgiving than beer but not by much. Sustained heat ages wine fast and can push out corks. Ask your importer where the wine will be stored between the port and the shop. Ask at what temperature too.

Licensed warehouses differ by state. Check which ones can hold imported wine and whether they offer temperature control. A cheap warehouse that cooks the wine is no saving.

Ask for a sample from the first shipment to be opened in India. Taste it against a bottle kept at home. If the two differ, find out where the damage happened before you send the second container.

Keep a record of dates, storage sites and temperatures for each shipment. If a batch fails you will want to know where. The same records help you argue with a carrier or insurer. They also help you plan the next shipment with more confidence.

Start with a modest first order. A small shipment that arrives sound and sells through teaches more than a full container that sits unsold in a warehouse.
faqs: Can a foreign winery import wine itself?
Generally an Indian importer holds the registrations and licences. Take legal advice on the structure that fits you.
Are import rules the same in every state?
No. Customs rules are central, but licences, duties and sales rules are set by each state and change.
How do I protect wine from heat during shipping?
Use temperature-controlled containers and storage where you can. Keep the route short. Heat damage appears quickly.
